newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU set to clear AT&T link with Unisource.
newsitem.headline: EU set to clear AT&T link with Unisource.

text.p: The European Commission said on Friday it was ready to clear the Uniworld telecommunications alliance between U.S. phone giant AT&T and Europe's Unisource joint venture.
It said it was also ready to clear the involvement of Spain's Telefonica in Unisource, which also groups Dutch PTT Telecom BV, Sweden's Telia AB and Swiss Telecom PTT.
The Commission said it would give interested parties one month to comment before taking final decisions.
Separately, the Commission cleared a deal under which Dutch PTT Telecom and Telia will acquire 20 percent of Ireland's Telecom Eireann, thus sharing control with the Irish government.
It said Ireland's plans to liberalise its telecoms market meant Telecom Eireann would not strengthen its current market position.

In the Uniworld/Unisource deals, the EU executive noted that both Spain and Switzerland had also agreed to liberalise their telecoms markets and that AT&T had agreed to several conditions to win approval of the deals.

The U.S. company agreed to advise the Commission promptly of any complaint filed with the U.S. Federal Communications Commission about access to its international facilities -- and of the FCC's decision.

It also agreed that its "accounting rates" -- charges for completing foreign phone calls -- for other companies would be no higher than the lowest rate offered to any Unisource shareholder, the Commission said.
The Commission said Switzerland had agreed to fully open its market to competition by January 1, 1998 and Spain by November 30, 1998.
It noted Spain had already adopted legislation establishing a second telecoms operator, Retevision, and planned to grant a third license before January 1998.
It said Madrid also planned to enact legislation before end 1997 allowing additional licences for voice telephone service and public infrastructure to be requested from August 1998.
Switzerland has agreed to enact a law to liberalise its market fully by the start of 1998 in line with a deadline agreed by the EU for most of its members, the Commission said.
It had already granted 15 pilot licences allowing competitors of the state monopoly to provide some telecoms services -- such as Internet access and data transmission.
Commission spokesman Willy Helin told reporters the Commission was likely to make its final decision in early February.

In the Irish case, the Commission said 38 licensed providers were already offering value-added telecoms services in Ireland and that a GSM operator would start to operate soon. It said Ireland planned to fully liberalise its market by January 2000. -- Brussels Newsroom 32 2 287 6800
